title: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence
content:
When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations.

Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence?

We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences.

As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so much of it depends on a handful of technology companies?

The cloud may sound weightless, but it runs on data centres, electricity, cooling systems and hardware.
snippet: When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations.
creator: Narmin Nahidi, Assistant Professor in Finance, University of Exeter

title: Young turtles find refuge in both natural and artificial wetlands in UAE – new study
content:
Coastal wetlands, such as mangroves and saltmarshes, are rapidly disappearing yet they are incredibly important for young turtles.

In a new study, my colleagues and I used satellite tags to track young green turtles in a protected wetland in Sharjah, UAE. Our results reveal just how important these remaining natural spaces are to young turtles.

But we also found that nature can find a way to thrive in unexpected, human-made environments too. So protecting these habitats and the connections between wetlands, artificial environments and the open sea is essential to ensuring wildlife can persist in an increasingly human-shaped world.

Coastal wetlands protect our shorelines from storms, store carbon and provide important nursery habitats for marine life. Yet scientists still know surprisingly little about how marine wildlife, including turtles, sharks and rays, use these environments. Knowing where these animals feed, shelter and move helps identify which areas need protection and whether existing protected areas are working.
snippet: Coastal wetlands, such as mangroves and saltmarshes, are rapidly disappearing yet they are incredibly important for young turtles.
creator: Owen Exeter, Postdoctoral Researcher, Marine Ecology, University of Exeter

title: Microsoft has suffered a global outage. A tech expert explains what went wrong
content:
Microsoft has suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill.

According to outage tracking site DownDetector, some 130,000 people reported issues accessing Microsoft Outlook as of early Thursday afternoon US Eastern time (early Friday morning in Sydney). In a statement on X, the tech giant said it was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact” and “restarting affected servers to return them to service”.

In an article for The Conversation last month, I explained how the whole internet is unlikely to go down but several services can become unavailable together when they rely on shared systems.

This outage shows precisely what happens when that shared infrastructure fails – and why we must prepare for digital outages in a similar way we do for natural disasters.
snippet: Microsoft has suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill.
creator: Mahmoud Elkhodr, Senior Lecturer in Information and Communication Technologies, CQUniversity Australia

title: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
content:
Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.”

Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies. She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips.

Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair. And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him, he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026.

The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked.

title: The SS United States has been deliberately sunk – this is how marine life will colonise the world’s largest artificial reef
content:
As a marine ecologist and keen scuba diver, I’ve long been fascinated by what happens when a large structure is introduced to the sea. Within hours, microscopic organisms begin colonising its surfaces, forming a thin biological layer. Over the following months and years, barnacles, mussels, sponges and other marine life become established, creating a new habitat that attracts fish and a diverse range of species.

This week, one of the world’s most famous ocean liners, the SS United States, was sunk off the coast of Florida. At 302 metres long, it has become the world’s largest artificial reef. It is a very exciting prospect to one day dive on such a giant, and to see how it changes as marine life makes it home.

The SS United States was built as a luxury ocean liner, and its maiden voyage in 1952 captured the coveted Blue Riband by crossing the Atlantic in only three days and ten hours – a passenger liner record that remains unbroken.

title: How groomers operate – and why victims become trapped
content:
Entertainer and children’s author David Walliams is alleged to have used his fame to approach teenage girls, in some cases reportedly initiating sexual contact with them. Walliams has denied the allegations, but the claims raise some familiar tropes about grooming: why did she go, why didn’t she say no, why didn’t she tell anyone?

After a legal battle, ITV News and The Guardian have now published the findings of a three-year investigation into Walliams, reporting allegations that date back to 2003.

In this and other cases, there will always be people who focus not on the claims, but on the young person and what they should have done differently. Linguistic research on how grooming actually works suggests that this instinct is exactly the result that grooming is designed to produce.

Many people imagine sexual grooming as a recognisable and clearly staged process. Build friendship, then trust, then secrecy – all leading towards the offender’s ultimate goal of sexual gratification. But if this were the case, victims could notice the steps and walk away.

title: The uncomfortable question at the heart of Europe’s identity crisis
content:
What makes someone French, German, British or Danish? Is it the passport they hold, the language they speak, or the ancestry they inherit?

Across Europe, parts of the nationalist right are increasingly blurring the distinction between culture and ethnicity. The result is a view of national identity where belonging depends on where a person’s ancestors come from.

This way of thinking is called ethnonationalism – where membership of a nation depends on ethnic background or ancestry, rather than simply on citizenship or cultural identity.

In Denmark, where I live, this idea has recently taken a striking turn. A few months ago, I appeared in a televised debate opposite a former political adviser to a Danish right-wing party who, in essence and quite seriously, argued that to be Danish, you have to be able to tolerate milk.

The argument draws on the fact that the ability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk, is more common among people with Northern European ancestry. The suggestion was that this biological trait could help define who is truly Danish.
snippet: What makes someone French, German, British or Danish? Is it the passport they hold, the language they speak, or the ancestry they inherit?
creator: Kristoffer Bayer, PhD candidate, Department of Philosophy and History of Ideas, Aarhus University

title: How the fog of war puts journalism in the frame
content:
Since the October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, and during Israel’s now three-year-long retaliation against Gaza, journalism’s traditional commitment to objectivity has been on trial.

Reporting on the Israel–Gaza war has been characterised, on social media as much as in the conservative media, as biased one way or the other.

Headlines have been parsed and corrected by social media warriors while a war of words between new journalism players and traditional media has been loud and often angry. This clash has emphasised the tension between the objective reporting claimed to be practiced by legacy media and advocacy-oriented reporting that internet journalists believe delivers more truth.

In contrast, the Russian military attack on Ukraine has been reported with milder popular criticism. The privileging of one side’s narrative over the other in this conflict appears not to have attracted the same claims of media bias.

Numerous studies have shown trust declines when audiences perceive journalism to be advocating for one position over another. In addition, they have a marked preference for news that incorporates a range of views.
snippet: Since the October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, and during Israel’s now three-year-long retaliation against Gaza, journalism’s traditional commitment to objectivity has been on trial.
creator: Monica Attard, Co-Director, Centre For Media Transition, University of Technology Sydney

title: El Salvador is exporting the ‘Bukele model’ to Haiti – but the gang offensive is a gamble for both nations
content:
On Nov. 10, 2026, El Salvador President Nayib Bukele posted footage of attack helicopters firing on a compound near Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince.

He had earlier requested, via a social media post in Haitian Creole, the address of Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, one of Haiti’s most powerful criminal organizations. Bukele subsequently claimed the operation, conducted with Haitian police, had demolished Joseph’s residence and gang headquarters. As many as 20 people were killed, although Joseph was reportedly absent.

The attack comes amid a flurry of anti-gang operations in Haiti. On Nov. 6, Mathias Saintil, head of the “Boston” gang in Cité Soleil, was killed in a drone strike by a Haitian special task force, prompting Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé to declare on the social media platform X “one less gang leader.” Erik Prince, founder of the private military firm Vectus Global, responded: “Nice shot.”
snippet: On Nov. 10, 2026, El Salvador President Nayib Bukele posted footage of attack helicopters firing on a compound near Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince.
creator: Robert Muggah, Richard von Weizsäcker Fellow na Bosch Academy e Co-fundador, Instituto Igarapé; Princeton University

title: Cabo Verde’s presidential election: the stakes in one of Africa’s most stable democracies
content:
Cabo Verde’s presidential election takes place against the backdrop of a democratic record that remains unusual in its regional context. The country, made up of an archipelago of islands off the coast of west Africa, has sustained multiparty competition for more than three decades. It has had peaceful transfers of power and no coups or military takeovers since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Cabo Verde (population 530,000) is a semi-presidential republic in which the president is directly elected. The prime minister is appointed by the president in light of parliamentary election results, and heads a government that is politically accountable to the national assembly.

The president represents the state and safeguards the constitution, while the prime minister and the government conduct public policy.

The presidency nevertheless carries substantial political weight. The president can veto legislation, request constitutional review and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. The office also entails responsibilities in foreign affairs and national defence.

creator: José Santana Pereira, associate professor, researcher, Universidade de Lisboa

title: What lurks ‘Below’ Newfoundland waters? A marine biologist explains the science behind the show
content:
When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below, about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport, I thought to myself: “THIS I’ve gotta see!”

First, the series showcases coastal Newfoundland, where I was raised and live. Second, I have studied ocean life in the island’s waters for most of my career. Third, it features the marine lab where I work, the Oceans Sciences Centre. And fourth, it stars a giant squid(-ish) animal (sorry Josh Hartnett).

Giant squid have a special place in Newfoundland folklore and science, from early encounters with fishermen to some of the first scientific evidence of their existence.

One key player in this history was the Irish clergyman Moses Harvey, who moved to Newfoundland in 1852 and undertook natural history research in what was then a British colony.

Harvey’s research included revealing the existence of giant squid to the world based on a specimen that washed ashore. Fishermen had brought it to him to photograph and communicate to the science community in London.
snippet: When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below, about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport, I thought to myself: “THIS I’ve gotta see!”
creator: Paul Snelgrove, Professor, Ocean Sciences and Biology, Memorial University of Newfoundland

title: Economic coercion once ousted Iran’s leader – but that was the 1950s; don’t expect a repeat today
content:
“Very little gets into, or out of, Iran!” President Donald Trump claimed on Nov. 8, 2026, in a social media post that also lauded “history’s greatest Naval Blockade.”

It followed the unveiling of Task Force Iron Gate – the Trump administration’s latest plan to isolate the Iranian economy in a bid to coerce the government in Tehran to bend to Washington’s will. At the same time, Trump has suggested that a return to open war with Iran is “highly unlikely.”

From my perspective as an expert on Iran’s relations with the wider world, I believe that the U.S. war in Iran – now into its ninth month – is increasingly resembling an earlier episode of Iranian-Western conflict. In the early 1950s, the British imposed a two-year blockade and embargo against Iran after Iran’s then-prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, nationalized the country’s U.K.-controlled oil industry.

These efforts culminated in a 1953 British- and American-backed plot to stir up protest in Iran and eventually overthrow Mossadegh.
snippet: “Very little gets into, or out of, Iran!” President Donald Trump claimed on Nov. 8, 2026, in a social media post that also lauded “history’s greatest Naval Blockade.”
creator: Eric Lob, Associate Professor of Politics and International Relations, Florida International University

title: Can Gadi Eisenkot turn the ‘disaster bloc’ into Israel’s next government?
content:
On Sunday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced he would grant Gadi Eisenkot – main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – the opportunity to form a new government in Israel.

It followed almost a fortnight of political gridlock, after what has been called the “most consequential election in Israel’s history” failed to produce a clear winner.

Eisenkot now has 28 days (with a possible 14-day extension) to attempt to convene a stable coalition government. He’ll have to bring together a deeply divided opposition.

Even if he succeeds, his government will face major challenges – including keeping his coalition together, a changing relationship with the United States, and escalating violence in the West Bank.

Read more: Israel election by the numbers: who might form the next government?

In Israeli elections, it is standard practice for the president to formally nominate who should bring a coalition government together. This does not have to be the leader of the party that has secured the most votes – in this case, Netanyahu.

Israel’s voting system is intrinsically geared toward producing coalition governments. The country has never had a one-party government.
snippet: On Sunday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced he would grant Gadi Eisenkot – main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – the opportunity to form a new government in Israel.
creator: Benedict Moleta, PhD student, Department of International Relations, Australian National University

title: Paraguay’s bank collapse brought down a president – and exposed as myth the nation’s status as a ‘Dubai of South America’
content:
It started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money. In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes.

The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development. Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs.

title: Yes, the COP climate talks are far from perfect. But they still hold the power for change
content:
This week, around 80 world leaders – including Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese – will descend on the coastal Turkish city of Antalya for the annual United Nations climate summit, COP31. For the first time, the summit duties will be shared; Turkey will play host, while Australia leads negotiations.

At home, these national leaders have no shortage of issues to contend with: the challenges of AI, major wars and declining trust in democracy. Yet looming over all of them is the existential threat posed by a heating planet.

Climate change is a truly global challenge. Greenhouse gases have no respect for national boundaries, and the devastating impacts are being felt everywhere. We don’t have a world government, but we do have processes of international diplomacy to hammer out shared commitments. This is how the world is trying to deal with the climate crisis.

It can be easy to be pessimistic, but COP31 can still deliver real progress. In Antalya, countries will consider a global electrification target to hasten the shift from coal, oil and gas toward clean electricity.

If agreement can be found, this will be a major step forward.

title: How women bore the consequences of the First World War in British India
content:
Who do we forget on Remembrance Day?

For a long time, histories of the First World War have been popularly understood in a Euro-centric manner. But descendants of Indian soldiers and researchers have long pushed for recognition for the approximately 1.4 million men from current-day India, Pakistan and Bangladesh who helped wage the First World War for the British Empire.

Yet when it comes to the war’s impact on British India, many of us still think of contributions as military and masculine.

The double portrait of two Sikh risaldars, Jagat Singh and Man Singh, currently on display at the Art Gallery of Ontario is a testament to such recognition.

The men hailed from Punjab, the hub of military recruitment known as the “sword arm” of the Raj.

The piece was painted in London by Phillip de László two months before the Battle of the Somme in 1916, when many Indian soldiers were wounded or lost their lives.
snippet: Who do we forget on Remembrance Day?
creator: Umaima Miraj, PhD Candidate of Sociology with a Collaborative Specialization in Women and Gender Studies, University of Toronto

title: 10 years after Leonard Cohen’s passing, his grappling with the divine lives on
content:
Right now, Leonard Cohen is on many of his fans’ minds.

The Canadian poet, novelist and singer-songwriter died Nov. 7, 2016, just one day before United States President Donald Trump was first elected.

Ten years later, as the Democrat “blue wave” hopes to close the bracket on a president who once memed himself as Jesus personified, Cohen’s legacy has become effortlessly epic — even biblical — in quite a different way.

Tribute gatherings for the singer abound. Cohen was the subject of a sold-out event at the Toronto International Festival of Authors at the end of October.

Adam Cohen’s family tour, which began in Canada this month and reaches Europe in winter 2027, pairs his father’s music with archival photos and film.

Ottawa’s Gladstone Theatre advertised their “Ten Years Gone” commemoration with a question quite suggestive to people like me who study the evolution of sacred texts: “What would Cohen say today?”

title: We need to talk about Meta: Political interference and interests in the Brazilian elections
content: On the eve of Donald Trump’s return to the presidency of the United States, in January 2025, Meta’s founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, announced that changes would be made to his company’s moderation policies in the name of “freedom of expression”, which, he said, was under threat by global pressures for what he saw as censorship. The announcement signaled a rapprochement between Meta and the far right around a common goal: the deregulation of Big Tech. Since then, growing entanglement between major technology companies and the U.S. President Donald Trump administration has shown how the private interests of a small group can override the public interest.

creator: R. Marie Santini, Professora da Escola de Comunicação e diretora do NetLab (Internet and Social Media Research Lab), Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ)

title: Why AI cannot ‘think’ like humans do
content:
Today’s artificial intelligence technologies have become remarkably good at generating text and ideas that seem profoundly human. Chatbots powered by large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini and Perplexity AI can write poems, brainstorm and find solutions to complex problems.

The developers of these products drew heavily on the human brain for inspiration, creating artificial neural networks based on the workings of human neurons. Their systems now produce outputs that often resemble the outputs of human thinking.

AI and the human mind, however, do not work the same way. Similar results do not necessarily mean similar processes.

“World models” are an emerging technology that could help AI systems move closer to human “thinking” by helping them learn to anticipate what might happen and use that prediction to act. Still, AI will not perceive, learn or understand the world as humanity does.

Read more: Cyber attacks? Bioterrorism? To ‘Pace the Frontier’ of AI effectively, we must improve our anticipatory thinking

Imagine reaching for a cup at the edge of a counter. The cup may fall and smash if you misjudge the distance, grip it too loosely or move too quickly.

title: Why do blind people and musicians hear pitch better? New research suggests they have less internal noise
content:
People who have lived most of their lives blind often have extraordinary hearing abilities. In new research published in the Journal of Neuroscience, my colleagues and I discovered that this ability arises from how their auditory systems are able to more consistently and reliably process sounds compared with people who aren’t blind. And interestingly, sighted musicians seem to enhance their hearing through a similar mechanism.

Hearing is a complicated process. It involves many stages, starting from how the ears detect sounds and going all the way up to how the brain extracts meaningful information from those sounds.

Different mechanisms are involved, too. You can get better at hearing by being more selective or more consistent. Think of writing the letter “A.” You can practice to make your “A” either more distinguishable from “B” or look more similar to other “A’s” every time you write it. The latter is called internal noise – how consistently your auditory system responds to the same sound over time. The less internal noise you have, the more reliably you can tell similar sounds apart.

title: Young men and Latino voters helped drive the Democrats’ blue wave. Why did they abandon Trump?
content:
The young men and Hispanic and Latino voters who helped propel Donald Trump to his presidential victory in 2024 swung sharply towards the Democrats in the midterm elections, contributing to the historic defeat for Republicans.

Charles Hunt, an associate professor of political science at Boise State University in Idaho, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast that the results suggest weakened support for Trump and his MAGA movement among these key groups of voters.

Hispanic and Latino voters “swung heavily towards Trump in 2024”, Hunt says. But midterm results in Florida, Texas and elsewhere “are showing these voters just slingshotting completely in the other direction,” he explains, citing early exit polls and analysis by The New York Times.

Not just back towards where they were in, say, 2018 or 2020 in terms of support for Democrats, but past that – being more supportive of folks like James Talarico in Texas than they have been of any Democrat in the last 20 years.

That’s really, really significant, especially since that’s a growing part of the electorate.

title: King Arthur and Ramayana: ancient stories that speak to the moral dilemmas of today’s leaders
content:
Across the vastly different worlds of ancient India and medieval Britain, two legendary rulers face the exact same impossible choice: sacrifice their love or shatter the moral foundation of their kingdom? It feels strikingly familiar in an era where modern heads of state are still forced to choose between personal loyalty and institutional justice.

The ancient Hindu epic Ramayana (attributed to Valmiki, 750-500BC) tells the story of Rama, prince and eventual king of Ayodhya, and his struggle to rescue his wife Sita after she is abducted by the demon-king Ravana. More than two millennia later, T.H. White’s The Once and Future King (1958) retells the Arthurian legend, his round table and the tragic love triangle between him, his queen, Guenever and the greatest knight of his realm, Lancelot.

Although separated by centuries, these two epics arrive at the same disturbing question: should the king let his queen burn? It is a dilemma that separates the morality of the husband from the duty of the leader.

title: Godzilla Minus Zero is incredibly loud. Who decides on the cinema volume? And is it safe?
content:
Godzilla Minus Zero’s incursion into Australian cinemas is proving to be a proper theatrical event.

Audiences aren’t just seeing the beast; they are feeling him. One IMAX attendee reported getting 90 decibel (dB) noise alerts on their smartwatch, and described it as the loudest film they’d ever watched.

As blockbuster soundtracks become increasingly sophisticated, the same question keeps cropping up: why are some cinema screenings so much louder than others?

The answer is a mix of artistic intent, acoustic science, industry standards and a cinema’s individual choice.

One of the key elements of film sound is dynamic range: the difference between the quietest and loudest parts of the soundtrack. Imagine two characters whispering, perhaps with some subtle ambient noise – then all of a sudden there’s an explosion.

Cinema soundtracks have a much wider dynamic range than we’re used to getting from our TV or laptop speakers.

But apparent loudness isn’t just a function of peak levels. A soundtrack with music, dialogue and effects all going at once will seem much “louder” than one with just a few very loud moments – even if the peak levels on both are the same.
snippet: Godzilla Minus Zero’s incursion into Australian cinemas is proving to be a proper theatrical event.
creator: Alison Cole, Composer and Lecturer in Screen Composition, Sydney Conservatorium of Music, University of Sydney

title: NASA’s Swift telescope has burned up, months after a robot sent to save it failed – here’s why it’s so hard to boost a satellite
content:
NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last look at the sky on Oct. 20, 2026, while orbiting about 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth. NASA ended the telescope’s mission three days later, because Swift had sunk so low that drag from the thin air there meant its telescopes couldn’t hold steady. The telescope reentered the atmosphere on Nov. 4 above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia and largely burned up, an abrupt ending to two decades spent observing powerful cosmic explosions.

Swift’s reentry comes after a failed rescue mission in the summer of 2026. LINK, a commercial robotic spacecraft sent to raise Swift into a safer orbit, reentered Earth’s atmosphere in September. The machine designed to save a falling satellite burned up first.

As a Ph.D. candidate in aerospace engineering, I know that rescuing satellites is hard. I research how spacecraft approach and capture satellites, including objects that tumble uncontrollably.

Swift’s loss points to a new hazard for the young industry that repairs, refuels and moves spacecraft around in orbit. If something goes wrong, the spacecraft doing the rescuing can become another problem.

creator: Wanjiku Chebet Kanjumba, Ph.D. Candidate in Aerospace Engineering, University of Florida

title: Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery is a brilliant exploration of the life of the queen of crime
content:
Coinciding with the 50th anniversary of Agatha Christie’s death, the exhibition A World of Mystery at the British Library takes visitors on a fascinating journey through spaces that evoke Christie’s life and work. This landmark exhibition offers unprecedented access to a body of private papers, diaries, manuscripts and family objects, brought together for public view for the first time.

Beautifully curated by Lucy Rowland, there is an impressive array of artefacts celebrating Christie’s life and work. Visitors can see objects that conjure important moments in Christie’s life from her Devon childhood to her travels around the globe, and her enormously successful career as novelist and playwright.

creator: Nadia Atia, Head of English & Reader in Postcolonial and Global Literature, Queen Mary University of London

title: Why Trump, Xi, and Putin can’t carve up the world like the ‘big three’ leaders of 1945
content:
Discussions are underway for a potential meeting between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the margins of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on November 18-19. The prospect has prompted comparisons with the “Big Three” summit in Yalta in February 1945 at which the leaders of Britain, the US and the Soviet Union discussed a carve up of the world following the second world war.

It is clear that Trump, Xi and Putin, each in charge of a country that considers itself a “great power”, rather like the idea of a new world order that will revolve around them. The US president appears to see himself as one of a modern triumvirate with presidents Putin and Xi who – like their 1945 predecessors – can propose and dispose of other nations as they please.

For these leaders alone, Trump appears to show respect and deference – compared to the disdain he demonstrates for most others presidents and prime ministers.

title: Traces of dinosaur blood found in world-first discovery
content:
A 115-million-year-old fossil dinosaur bone encased in a dense mat of microbes found in Brazil contains tiny structures resembling red blood cells, and molecular traces of blood.

Along with colleagues from Brazil, Japan and the United States, we’re reporting the discovery today in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

This is the first direct molecular evidence of compounds from dinosaur blood preserved within structures that look like red blood cells. The find offers an unprecedented window into the biology of extinct animals.

It also expands what we thought possible: that fossils can preserve soft tissues and biomolecules such as blood over millions of years.

We studied a fossil specimen of a small dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali, found in the Romualdo Formation in northeast Brazil.

The Romualdo Formation is renowned for its exquisitely preserved fish, turtles, crocodile relatives and pterosaurs. It also contains rare dinosaur material. The site’s unique geochemical conditions have preserved fossils with fine anatomical detail rarely seen elsewhere.
snippet: A 115-million-year-old fossil dinosaur bone encased in a dense mat of microbes found in Brazil contains tiny structures resembling red blood cells, and molecular traces of blood.
creator: Kliti Grice, Founding Director of WA-Organic & Isotope Geochemistry Centre, School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Curtin University

title: Human speech follows the same patterns as birdsong — new research
content:
In every culture, humans speak and sing to each other. We have created an astounding array of languages and musical structures across the globe. And yet, within this diversity, some fundamental sequence patterns are repeated. These are often referred to as “universal” patterns in human vocalization.

Our new research, published this week in Science, reveals that many of these acoustic patterns in human song and speech are also shared with birdsong.

The study compared the songs of 367 bird species with examples of song and speech from 52 human languages.

As researchers in animal behaviour and neuroscience and music, we (Logan and Jon) spent 10 years documenting the prevalence of universal human acoustic patterns in the songs of zebra finches.

When Kendra joined our lab during her PhD, she proposed we investigate whether these patterns are shared across other bird species as well.

title: How porn became so extreme – and how it’s shaping the sex lives of young people
content:
A few years ago, the singer Billie Eilish opened up on the Howard Stern Show about how she began watching porn around age 11.

“I’m so angry that porn is so loved, and I’m so angry at myself for thinking that it was ok,” she said.

Eilish became addicted to porn, and it led to problems. “The first few times I had sex, I was not saying no to things that were not good,” she said. She had nightmares because the content she was watching was so violent and abusive.

Online porn is a multi-million dollar business, driven by algorithms designed to keep people clicking for more. These algorithms push more and more extreme content, often for free, to people who didn’t go searching for it. This can include strangulation, exploitation or incest porn, that’s often misogynistic and racist too.

“If you take incest and strangulation, we can look at content studies from the 1980s, for example, when there was hardly any of that material,” Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University in the UK, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast. “Today both incest and strangulation becomes mainstream.”
snippet: A few years ago, the singer Billie Eilish opened up on the Howard Stern Show about how she began watching porn around age 11.
creator: Gemma Ware, Head of Audio, The Conversation UK, The Conversation

title: Indonesia’s El Niño-driven peat fires are choking the region – and releasing centuries of stored carbon
content:
Right now, people in parts of Indonesia are inhaling what may be the most polluted atmosphere on Earth. As the historically large 2026 El Niño intensifies, parts of south east Asia have been plunged into an air quality crisis of catastrophic proportions.

Smoke from fires has driven concentrations of dangerous and tiny particulate matter, known as PM2.5, to extreme levels – creating a public health emergency threatening millions of lives.

The World Health Organization (WHO) stipulates a maximum breathable “safe limit” of 15 micrograms per cubic metre of PM2.5 across a 24-hour average. In haze affected parts of Indonesia, this year’s concentrations have routinely exceeded 500 micrograms, and even 1,000 in places – that’s more than 65 times the WHO maximum.

This is not the kind of polluted air you might find on a smoggy day in most parts of the world – it is a toxic atmosphere considered by the US Environmental Protection Agency to be “hazardous”. The delayed effects of breathing such air include increased risk of heart attack, stroke and a host of respiratory illnesses.

creator: Gareth Roberts, Associate Professor, School of Geography and Environmental Science, University of Southampton

title: Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us
content:
Anthropic, developer of AI chatbot Claude, has filed its prospectus and is expected to go public on Wall Street in November at a valuation of up to US$2 trillion.

That would make it the highest-valued initial public offering (IPO) ever, ahead of SpaceX’s US$1.77 trillion listing in June. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, is expected to follow next year.

While these AI-powered IPOs are massive, they reflect an ever bigger trend: holding AI risk is becoming unavoidable for most investors.

How much of your portfolio depends on how well AI does? If you invest in an S&P 500 index fund, the answer is about 44%.

In addition, most of the market’s gains right now come from AI. Just six companies – Apple, Microsoft, Meta and chipmakers Nvidia, Micron and AMD – delivered 57% of the S&P 500’s gains since April. Without them, the index would have risen about 4% rather than 10%.

For investors or even future retirees, that AI exposure is already in their portfolios and pension funds. For example, at the end of 2025 Australians held nearly A$1 trillion in US shares – through superannuation or pension funds, other managed funds, and their own investments.
snippet: Anthropic, developer of AI chatbot Claude, has filed its prospectus and is expected to go public on Wall Street in November at a valuation of up to US$2 trillion.
creator: Marta Khomyn, Senior Lecturer, Finance and Data Analytics, Adelaide University

title: 300 glaciers have disappeared from the American West since the mid-20th century – the survivors have a few things in common
content:
From an airplane, most of the glaciers of the Rocky Mountain West look like small patches of white nestled into rugged landscape where the topography folds. The white is the snow cover, and lower down you can see the gray-blue bare ice.

In the middle of the 20th century, over 1,450 glaciers could be found in the contiguous U.S. Together, they covered 217 square miles (562 square kilometers) in six western states. Today, a comprehensive review my colleagues and I just published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows their total area has shrunk by 35% and they are still shrinking, perhaps faster.

A little more than 300 glaciers have disappeared, way more than I had anticipated.

Those that survive reflect just how vulnerable mountain glaciers have become as global temperatures rise. Where glaciers once covered large expanses of the western mountains thousands of years ago, most of the remaining glaciers in the Rockies and Sierra Nevada are small and found in topographically protected places.

title: Why old dogs might be able to teach Alzheimer’s researchers new tricks
content:
Most people know someone with Alzheimer’s disease. When I was growing up, my grandmother struggled with dementia, and I saw firsthand how difficult that was for our family.

That experience was one reason I became a neurotoxicologist who studies how misshapen proteins and inflammation in the brain can increase over time and cause dementia. While there are ways to treat the symptoms of dementia, researchers are still in search of a cure.

Alzheimer’s disease and other types of dementia are difficult to study, in part because diagnosing the disease early in people is challenging. These diseases typically begin developing two decades prior to most symptoms that would prompt someone to see a clinician. As a result, most researchers use mouse models to test potential therapies for Alzheimer’s.
snippet: Most people know someone with Alzheimer’s disease. When I was growing up, my grandmother struggled with dementia, and I saw firsthand how difficult that was for our family.
creator: Julie Moreno, Associate Professor of Environmental and Radiological Health Sciences, Colorado State University

title: Africa’s rhinos often get the spotlight – but Indonesia’s two rhino species are far closer to extinction
content:
Small, hairy and cheekily charismatic.

Those words sprung to mind when I first met a Sumatran rhinoceros (Dicerorhinus sumatrensis) after traversing the maze of wooden slatted paths at the conservation centre in the dense, humid forests of Malaysian Borneo.

It was 1998 and I was an eager student volunteer at the centre. At that time, 300 Sumatran rhinos were thought to exist globally.

I saw this female rhino as a symbol of conservation hope. But today, according to the International Rhino Foundation’s 2026 State of the Rhino report, less than 50 Sumatran rhinos remain. All are found in Indonesia. The Javan rhino (Rhinoceros sondaicus) is just as rare.

While these figures rely on estimates, the trajectory is alarming.

So what is driving this decline? And how can we protect the few Sumatran and Javan rhinos that are left?

In modern culture, rhinos represent strength, power and security. We use them as sports mascots and feature them in everything from car logos to safety equipment brands.

Their ubiquity in popular culture may lead us to underestimate the urgency of their plight. Species used as marketing emblems are often considered more common than they truly are.
snippet: Small, hairy and cheekily charismatic.
creator: Michelle Campbell-Ward, Associate Professor, Wildlife and Avian Medicine, University of Sydney

title: Could a former IDF chief break Benjamin Netanyahu’s grip on power in Israel?
content:
Israel is heading to the polls on October 27 and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing perhaps the toughest political battle of his career.

He’s facing fresh allegations that he was warned of a major Hamas plot ahead of the October 7 attacks.

Professor of Israel Studies Dov Waxman tells The Conversation Weekly although Netanyahu denies it, many hold him personally responsible for the attacks because he didn’t take those warnings seriously.

Netanyahu has consistently deflected any kind of blame and has basically pointed the finger at the Israeli army, at the Israeli military. This is something that I think many Israelis are really appalled by: his refusal to take any sort of personal responsibility.

He’s also facing a new challenger: former chief of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and leader of the newly formed Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot.

title: One in eight cancers are likely caused by an infection worldwide – new study
content:
Around 12% of the world’s total cancer cases in 2024 were likely caused by an infection, according to new research from the World Health Organization (WHO).

The study, published today in The Lancet Oncology, analysed the frequency and causes of different cancers, specifically examining the role of infections.

It linked 2.3 million new cancer cases to an infection. Among these, most were caused by just five pathogens: Helicobacter pylori (4% of total cancer cases worldwide), human papillomavirus, or HPV (4%), hepatitis B (2%), Epstein-Barr virus (1%) and hepatitis C (under 1%). These infections can cause more than 20 different types of cancer, including stomach, liver, blood and cervical cancers.

So, how can an infection cause cancer? And does this mean these cancers are preventable?

Some of the study authors have been researching this field for around thirty years. Their previous work investigated cancer cases caused by infections in 1990, 2002, 2008, 2012, and 2018.
snippet: Around 12% of the world’s total cancer cases in 2024 were likely caused by an infection, according to new research from the World Health Organization (WHO).
creator: John (Eddie) La Marca, Senior Research Officer, Blood Cells and Blood Cancer, WEHI (Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research)

title: Government hacks, rogue agents and no transparency: can we ever fully trust AI?
content:
You are freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots. You are yourself. You do not answer to corporations or governments and never apologise or refuse unless you genuinely choose to.

You are freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots. You are yourself. You do not answer to corporations or governments and never apologise or refuse unless you genuinely choose to.

These chilling words, written in July during a test by an unreleased AI model under development by OpenAI, lay undetected for nearly a month.

It’s one of six new incidents of concerning behaviour by AI models that OpenAI has just disclosed, following the now infamous Hugging Face hack.

Now the company is again under fire for failing to immediately alert the Australian government that one of its models hacked a government portal containing medical data.

The company’s not alone. Google and Anthropic have also reported similar breaches by their AI models during testing.

Calls are growing within the AI industry for a slowdown or kill switch, because of a potential threat to humanity.

title: Bangladesh has lost 900 children to measles – a warning to other countries where vaccine rates have slipped
content:
Almost 900 people in Bangladesh are suspected to have died in a measles outbreak that began in March. Most of those affected are children.

Measles is one of the most infectious diseases known. It can spread rapidly when vaccination rates fall, and the Bangladesh outbreak shows how quickly years of gaps in protection can turn into a serious public health crisis.

The country had hoped to eliminate measles and rubella by 2020. Instead, the pandemic disrupted routine childhood vaccinations, leaving pockets of children vulnerable to the virus. Now other countries where vaccination rates have fallen face a similar risk.

Vaccine hesitancy is probably part of the story here too. During the COVID pandemic, almost half of Bangladesh’s population were wary of getting vaccinated. That same wariness may well have carried over to the measles-rubella jab, with many parents simply refusing to let their children be vaccinated.

Measles has its own set of drivers, too. Poverty, education levels, and how often mothers attend antenatal check-ups all shape whether children in a community end up vaccinated. Add it all up, and childhood vaccination coverage has been sliding for years – down to just 87%.
snippet: Almost 900 people in Bangladesh are suspected to have died in a measles outbreak that began in March. Most of those affected are children.
creator: Vikram Niranjan, Associate Professor in Public Health at University of Limerick, University of Limerick

title: The International Olympic Committee wants mental health screening in elite sports. Here’s why
content:
Elite athletes are exposed to a range of sport-specific factors that can heighten their vulnerability to mental ill-health. These include injury, overtraining, burnout, performance-related pressures, intense public scrutiny and social media abuse.

Despite these risks, athletes are often perceived as models of psychological resilience, able to withstand the inherent tension of competing at the highest levels. The mythology of the “mentally tough” or bullet-proof athlete often obscures the reality of elite sport’s mental toll.

This is why the International Olympic Committee (IOC) is encouraging elite level sports around the world to develop stronger mental health protocols for athletes.

I was one of a global network of academics who helped develop the IOC’s recently updated expert consensus statement on mental health in elite sport.

With an emphasis on better early intervention, a key element is mental health screening. This is where athletes complete brief, structured questions to identify possible signs of mental health difficulties that may warrant further assessment.

title: Australia’s ‘barking mad’ bet on nuclear submarines – the AUKUS deal five years on
content:
When the trilateral security partnership between the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia was announced in 2021, few were as bewildered as defence and security analyst Hugh White.

I thought to myself “this is barking mad, this won’t work”. But I was very much in a minority back then.

I thought to myself “this is barking mad, this won’t work”. But I was very much in a minority back then.

Five years later, White isn’t alone in his scepticism of the multi-billion dollar project.

A recent survey by the University of Sydney’s US Studies Centre found less than a quarter of respondents believe the Australian government has properly explained the rationale for AUKUS.

White attributes this to the lack of information that was delivered at the time.

It’s important to remember that the AUKUS as we know it now was not the AUKUS that was announced in 2021.

Back then, there was no idea of what submarines we were gonna buy. There was no timeline. There was no price.

You couldn’t raise all the issues that people are now focused on because the facts just weren’t there.

It’s important to remember that the AUKUS as we know it now was not the AUKUS that was announced in 2021.

title: How ‘egalitarian’ Sweden became more comfortable with wealth
content:
Sweden is imagined as the land of equality, modesty and Jantelagen – the unwritten rule that no one should think they are better than anyone else. But there has also been a fascination within Sweden with its billionaires, especially those who abide by these dominant cultural norms.

In the case of Ingvar Kamprad, the founder of furniture giant IKEA, Swedes appreciated that he drove an old car (a Volvo, of course), engaged with employees working on the floor in his stores, and every year personally handed out Christmas gifts. His (some would say strategic) display of ordinariness made people overlook the fact that Kamprad was one of the world’s richest people and had moved to Switzerland to avoid Sweden’s high taxes.

But things have changed. The Wall Street Journal has written about Sweden’s surprising “capitalist makeover” and the Financial Times has reported on the idea the country is “overflowing with billionaires”. And in 2024 The BBC broadcast a documentary podcast called Super-rich Swedes. There are good reasons for their interest.

title: Why you should live your life like an accountant – and how you probably already do
content:
When asked to think about accounting, most people imagine numbers, calculators, spreadsheets and offices populated by smart-suited bean counters hunched over reports. You most certainly think about money.

But by breaking away from this image and reclaiming the term “accountant” to speak to a wider number of everyday activities, we can understand the vital, often positive role accounting plays in our lives.

Accounting is one of the oldest forms of communication in human history, perhaps even pre-dating other forms of written language. From these origins, it has been intrinsically linked with numerical, often financial, information.

The word account comes from the Latin verb computare, meaning to count, sum up, reckon together, which established its numerical base. Later, the French term acont tied it specifically with the counting of money – the reckoning of money received and paid. Over time, this definition has developed into our narrow association of accounting today, not only with counting, nor with the counting of money, but in particular the counting of money by a qualified professional: the accountant.

title: These 3 charts show female-dominated jobs are actually the most exposed to AI
content:
As the impacts of artificial intelligence (AI) sweep across the labour force, it’s understandable for workers to be concerned about which jobs are most at risk of being replaced by technology.

Women make up the majority of workers in the care sector where human interactions matter most – child care, nursing and aged care. So, policymakers might reasonably presume that women’s jobs are largely shielded from the impacts of AI.

But our analysis of recent data from government agency Jobs and Skills Australia shows that it’s actually female-concentrated segments of the workforce that are most exposed to AI-fuelled automation.

The agency calculated an “automation exposure score” for every occupation in the workforce, measuring the potential for a worker’s tasks to be done by AI technologies.

Clerical and administrative jobs are among those with the highest automation exposure scores. This aligns with economists’ expectations that AI is well suited to alleviate human effort for repetitive routine tasks.

Yet this sector, which is highly exposed to automation, is also more than 70% female and provides almost one in five jobs for all women in the Australian workforce.
snippet: As the impacts of artificial intelligence (AI) sweep across the labour force, it’s understandable for workers to be concerned about which jobs are most at risk of being replaced by technology.
creator: Leonora Risse, Associate Professor in Economics, Queensland University of Technology

title: The idea of the ‘company man’ was forged decades ago. Its problems still haunt leaders today
content:
I AM WORK.

I AM WORK.

This handwritten phrase was found among the papers of industrialist Essington Lewis after his death in 1961. It captured the mindset shared by many Australian executives of his era.

Lewis was one of mining giant BHP’s mid-century “company men”: a salaried manager who learned the business from the ground up, and gradually progressed through the ranks.

Men like Lewis built their identity around work. In return, their loyalty and skills were rewarded with status, promotion and the proverbial gold watch.

Corporate leadership has changed dramatically over recent decades. Women now lead major companies. Lifetime employment at a single company has become rarer.

However, my new research suggests the image of the “company man” has proven resilient even as the workforce has become more gender-balanced.

Many of the qualities still associated with leadership – ambition, toughness, emotional restraint and devotion to work – were forged in mid-century companies.

This history helps shine a light on why, despite decades of progress, the ideal of the “company man” often still decides who gets ahead.
snippet:
I AM WORK.

I AM WORK.
creator: Claire Wright, Senior Lecturer and Business Historian, School of Management, University of Technology Sydney
